notes.meaning: Ezekiel was sitting at home in Babylon fourteen months after his first vision. The elders of Judah were sitting before him, waiting to hear a message from God. Suddenly, the powerful hand and Spirit of the Lord came upon the prophet. God faithfully speaks to His people even when they are suffering far away in exile.

Ezekiel saw a glorious heavenly figure appearing like a man. From the waist down, the figure burned like fire, picturing God's holy anger against sin. From the waist up, He shone with brilliant, dazzling light, displaying the majesty of God.

The heavenly figure reached out what looked like a hand and lifted Ezekiel up by the hair of his head. The Holy Spirit carried him in a vision all the way to the temple in Jerusalem. Near the north gate of the inner court, Ezekiel saw an idol that provoked God to jealousy. This false god insulted the Lord by trying to steal the exclusive love and worship that belonged to Him alone.

In the very court where the idol stood, Ezekiel saw the bright glory of the God of Israel. It was the same majestic appearance he had seen earlier by the river in Babylon. Placing a worthless statue right next to the glorious presence of the living God showed how deeply Judah had insulted Him.

God told Ezekiel to look toward the north, and there the prophet saw the offensive idol at the entrance near the altar gate. Placed right along the path where people brought sacrifices to the Lord, this statue stood in open defiance of God. It tempted worshippers to turn away from the Lord the moment they entered His courts.

The Lord asked Ezekiel if he saw the terrible sins Israel was committing in His sacred courts. These shameful practices were driving God away from His own sanctuary, signaling that its protection would soon end. Yet the Lord warned Ezekiel that he would soon see sins that were even worse.

God brought Ezekiel to the entrance of the court, where the prophet noticed a hole in the wall. The people had put up barriers to hide their idolatry from the public eye. Sin often tries to hide behind a wall of secrecy, but nothing escapes God's notice.

God commanded Ezekiel to dig through the wall to make the opening larger. When the prophet dug, he discovered a secret doorway. Uncovering the hidden depths of sin often takes careful effort and searching.

The Lord instructed Ezekiel to step through the doorway and examine the wicked practices taking place inside. God was pulling back the cover on the secret deeds of Jerusalem's leaders. The Lord wanted His prophet to see clearly why His coming judgment was completely fair.

Inside the room, Ezekiel saw carvings and paintings of crawling creatures and unclean beasts covering the walls. These pictures reflected the animal gods of pagan nations, especially those worshipped in Egypt. Israel had abandoned the glorious Creator to bow down before drawings of reptiles and beasts.

Seventy elders of Israel stood in the dark room, burning thick clouds of incense before the animal carvings. Among them was Jaazaniah, a man from a respected family that had once supported Josiah's godly reforms. The very leaders who were supposed to guide the people into obedience were now leading the way in secret idolatry.

God pointed out that these elders carried out their worship in the dark, each in his own room of images. They justified their actions by claiming that the Lord did not see them and had abandoned the land. When people convince themselves that God is blind or uncaring, they feel free to plunge deeper into sin.

The Lord told Ezekiel to turn around again to see even greater abominations. Sin left unchecked does not stay still; it grows bolder and more destructive. God was continuing to reveal the full scope of Judah's spiritual rebellion.

At the northern gate of the temple, Ezekiel saw women sitting and weeping for Tammuz. Tammuz was a pagan fertility god whose worshippers believed he died and returned to life each year. Instead of weeping over their own sins before the true God, these women shed tears for a mythical dead idol.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe that church traditions like Lent and Easter originated from this ancient pagan mourning ritual for Tammuz.
Many evangelicals reject any link between Christian celebrations of the resurrection and Tammuz worship, arguing that claims of a pagan origin lack historical support.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic scholars state that celebrations of Christ's resurrection have no historic basis in the worship of Tammuz or ancient fertility myths.

notes.meaning: God asked Ezekiel if he had taken in this painful sight, and then promised to show him things that were even more offensive. Each layer of sin revealed in the vision was more shocking than the last. The Lord was proving that corruption had infected every part of Jerusalem's society.

Ezekiel was brought into the inner court, right between the porch and the altar where only priests were allowed to serve. There he saw about twenty-five men, likely leaders of the priesthood, standing with their backs turned against God's temple. Facing the east, they bowed down to worship the rising sun. They literally turned their backs on the Creator to adore the creature.

God asked Ezekiel whether Judah considered their awful deeds a small thing. Not only had they filled the entire land with violence against other people, but they also kept returning to the temple to insult God directly. Holding the branch to their nose refers to an insolent pagan ritual or a gesture of open contempt toward the Lord.

differ.view: Some in the Reformed tradition understand putting the branch to the nose figuratively as adding fuel to the fire, causing their own ruin by stirring up God's wrath.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholars note that holding a branch or flower to the nose may have been an ancient ritual gesture seen in Near Eastern star worship, though the exact meaning remains uncertain.

notes.meaning: Because Judah refused to turn from their wickedness, the Lord announced that He would judge them in wrath without any pity. Even if they screamed loudly for help when disaster struck, He would not listen to their cries. God looks for an upright and repentant heart, not merely loud shouts of panic when punishment arrives.
